executive_summary: A multi-dimensional analysis of the 37th Government's tenure reveals a profound structural dichotomy across two primary spheres: the extraordinary societal resilience, technological ingenuity, and operational military power demonstrated in neutralizing multi-front existential threats, contrasted with sub-par performance, institutional erosion, and sector-driven political priorities in the management of civilian, administrative, and public systems.

chapters.title: Macroeconomics, Fiscal Policy, and Credit Ratings
chapters.bottom_line: The Israeli macroeconomy demonstrated substantial structural resilience, averting a systemic debt crisis amidst war expenditures; however, government policy exacerbated fiscal vulnerabilities by preserving sectarian political allocations, damaging institutional credibility, and locking in a structural deficit that constrains long-term growth.
headlines: 8-percentage-point surge in debt-to-GDP ratio to ~68.5% in 2025
Record fiscal deficit of 6.8% of GDP in 2024
Unprecedented sovereign credit rating downgrades from Moody's, S&P, and Fitch
chapters.overview: Israel's fiscal trajectory underwent a sharp transition from the 2022 budget surplus of the 36th Government—which brought the debt-to-GDP ratio down to 60.5%—to an acute expansion of the fiscal deficit to 6.8% of GDP in 2024. This spike was driven overwhelmingly by war expenditures, pushing defense outlays to 8.3% of GDP. Public debt expanded to 67.8% of GDP by year-end 2024 and reached roughly 68.5% in 2025. Rating agencies downgraded Israel's credit score citing geopolitical vulnerability and fiscal uncertainty, though 2025 showed stabilization with 2.9% GDP growth and inflation receding to 2.6%.
chapters.comparison_prev_gov: The 36th Government eliminated the pandemic deficit through fiscal restraint and curtailed non-statutory coalition funds. In contrast, the 37th Government declined to dissolve redundant ministries and continued disbursing non-growth-enhancing coalition allocations, contributing to a medium-term structural deficit of ~3.6% of GDP.
chapters.arguments_supporters: The economy displayed resilience under extreme wartime shock; maintaining a debt-to-GDP ratio below 69% compares favorably with past international crises, and 2025's rebound to 2.9% growth and rate cuts proved the macroeconomic foundations held firm.
chapters.arguments_critics: Resilience stemmed from private high-tech dynamism and the Bank of Israel's $200B+ foreign reserves; the cabinet practiced fiscal populism by maintaining partisan coalition transfers, triggering credit downgrades and hundreds of millions in excess interest costs.

chapters.title: Cost of Living, Food Prices, and Consumer Basket
chapters.bottom_line: The 37th Government failed to curb the escalating cost of living. The confluence of elevated interest rates, supply disruptions, the VAT increase to 18%, and the absence of structural antitrust measures severely compressed Israeli household purchasing power.
headlines: 39% price level premium compared to the OECD average
VAT increased to 18% alongside frozen tax brackets
Over NIS 1,100 average monthly surge in mortgage repayments
chapters.overview: The cost of living remained the foremost concern for the Israeli voter, with price levels standing 38%–39% above the OECD average. Rate hikes to 4.75% expanded debt servicing, adding over NIS 1,100 monthly to an average mortgage compared to 2021. Food conglomerates and importers instituted cumulative price hikes exceeding 13% over three years, exploiting regulatory expirations, Turkish trade embargoes, and Red Sea Houthi attacks. The government raised VAT to 18% in 2025 and froze tax credit brackets, eroding real disposable income.
chapters.comparison_prev_gov: The 36th Government advanced market liberalization ('What is Good for Europe is Good for Israel') and agricultural tariff reductions. The 37th Government repealed disposable plastic and sugary beverage taxes as coalition concessions, while avoiding antitrust enforcement against major food cartels.
chapters.arguments_supporters: Inflationary spikes were the inevitable consequence of a regional war, Red Sea logistics crises, and the Turkish embargo; the government compensated via utility tariff subsidies and tax credits for parents of young children.
chapters.arguments_critics: The cabinet surrendered to major food cartels, failed to open parallel imports, and imposed regressive indirect taxation (18% VAT) while continuing to spend billions on redundant partisan ministries.

chapters.title: High-Tech Sector, Capital Raising, and Brain Drain
chapters.bottom_line: Israel's high-tech industry demonstrated remarkable vitality, regaining strong investment volumes; however, political instability accelerated structural shifts toward foreign corporate registration and the relocation of high-value human capital.
headlines: 150% surge in high-tech worker emigration in 2023
Over 60% of new startups incorporated abroad (Delaware)
Capital raising rebounded to $14.6 billion in 2025 (+30%)
chapters.overview: Following the 2021 funding peak ($25.6B) and 2022 global correction ($15B), local investments contracted sharply in 2023 to $8.0B due to judicial overhaul strife and the outbreak of war. The sector rebounded in 2024–2025, reaching $14.6B raised behind cybersecurity and AI demand. However, a major structural reallocation occurred: over 60% of new startups incorporated and registered IP in Delaware, tech worker emigration rose 150%, and companies established overseas satellite R&D centers to manage reserve-duty disruptions.
chapters.comparison_prev_gov: The 36th Government treated high tech as a primary national growth engine with regulatory fast-tracks. The 37th Government entered into open friction with industry leaders protesting the judicial overhaul, driving domestic capital flight.
chapters.arguments_supporters: The 2025 rebound to $14.6B invalidates claims of sector collapse; the Innovation Authority deployed fast-track grants and simplified foreign expert visas.
chapters.arguments_critics: Inflows were concentrated in a handful of mature cyber unicorns while early-stage startups faced a drought; widespread Delaware incorporation drains future exit tax revenues and moves executive jobs abroad permanently.

chapters.title: National Security, Battlefronts, and Regional Reconstruction
chapters.bottom_line: The government bears primary responsibility for the catastrophe of October 7, but subsequently prosecuted an offensive campaign that dismantled Iran's forward offensive ring around Israel. Nevertheless, the lack of a post-war diplomatic strategy for Gaza, Iran's continued nuclear expansion, and slow civilian reconstruction remain major strategic liabilities.
headlines: October 7 disaster: 1,200 murdered, 251 hostages, 100,000+ displaced
Over 86,000 newly recognized civilian victims of hostilities
Only 31% of the Tekuma Directorate reconstruction budget disbursed
chapters.overview: The security campaign encompassed three theaters: Gaza (dismantling Hamas brigades and eliminating Yahya Sinwar and Mohammed Deif, though lacking a day-after civilian governing plan), Lebanon (Operation Northern Arrows eliminating Hassan Nasrallah and Radwan invasion infrastructure), and direct Iranian missile barrages countered by historical interception rates and precision retaliatory strikes. Conversely, civilian reconstruction suffered severe delays: the Tekuma Directorate disbursed only NIS 5.4B of its NIS 17.4B budget by early 2026, and only 28% of returning residents felt secure.

rows: Collapse of containment; total war; eliminated leadership
Attrition war; Op Northern Arrows; degradation of Hezbollah
Interception of barrages; direct kinetic strikes inside Iran

chapters.comparison_prev_gov: The 36th Government operated under the assumption that economic incentives in Gaza and maritime gas agreements with Lebanon would secure quiet. The 37th Government maintained this containment until October 7, shifting thereafter to a decisive offensive doctrine.
chapters.arguments_supporters: The administration dismantled the Iranian axis of resistance ring, eliminated Nasrallah and Sinwar, re-established kinetic deterrence in Tehran, and saw 43 of 47 southern border communities resume operations.
chapters.arguments_critics: The cabinet ignored pre-war intelligence warnings and fractured societal deterrence; tactical triumphs were squandered without a viable day-after governing framework, leaving Hamas in partial civil control and Iran on the nuclear threshold.

chapters.title: Equitable Burden Sharing and Haredi Conscription Crisis
chapters.bottom_line: A deep rupture in the 'People's Army' ethos; modest total recruitment growth (4,300) was undermined by political refusal to enforce universal conscription, leaving ~72,000 draft-eligible men unintegrated amidst an acute military manpower deficit.
headlines: ~72,000 draft-eligible Haredi men classified as evaders
Only 1.2% compliance rate to direct personal draft notices (232 of 18,915)
Unprecedented reservist strain: 100–180 active duty days per year
chapters.overview: Following the expiration of deferment frameworks and the High Court of Justice ruling mandating universal conscription, the government avoided criminal or financial enforcement. While total Haredi enlistment reached 4,298 in 2025 (mostly working youth and older Stage-B reservists), compliance among full-time yeshiva students sent direct draft notices was almost zero (232 inductions). Concurrently, reservists suffered extraordinary exhaustion facing an immediate IDF deficit of 12,000 troops annually.
chapters.comparison_prev_gov: The 36th Government introduced progressive conscription targets with escalating institutional financial sanctions and lowering the exemption age to 21. The 37th Government pledged blanket statutory exemptions and pursued softened legislation without individual sanctions.
chapters.arguments_supporters: Total annual enlistment hit a record ~4,300 in 2025 (2.5x increase over 2022); coercion and criminalization cause mass unrest, and tailored units like the Hashmonaim Brigade offer the only sustainable path.
chapters.arguments_critics: Touting incremental figures masks systemic evasion by 72,000 men under political protection, placing the entire burden on exhausted reservists to preserve coalition survival.

chapters.title: Public Safety, Violent Crime, and Vehicle Thefts
chapters.bottom_line: Internal security experienced a significant deterioration: homicides within Arab society doubled, total nationwide murders hit historical peaks, and institutional trust in the police dropped, despite targeted progress in reducing vehicle thefts and expanding civilian defense licensing.
headlines: Historic peak of 252 homicides in Arab society in 2025 (+115% vs 2022)
Homicide clearance rate in Arab communities collapsed to 14.8%
Vehicle thefts dropped 19%–20% in 2025–2026 following previous record surges
chapters.overview: Violent crime surged across Israel, with national homicides rising from 142 in 2022 to 274 in 2023 and 263 in 2024. Arab communities endured unprecedented criminal syndicate warfare (252 murdered in 2025) with clearance rates falling below 15%. In property crime, vehicle thefts surged during 2023–2024 before receding ~20% in 2025 due to border seam patrols. Meanwhile, police faced heavy criticism as public-order protest arrests made up 75.6% of all detentions in 2024.
chapters.comparison_prev_gov: The 36th Government executed the 'Safe Route' inter-agency desk, reducing Arab sector homicides from 126 to 116. The 37th Government dismantled the integrated task force, entered open conflict with police leadership, and shifted priorities to protest policing.
chapters.arguments_supporters: Fast-tracked civilian firearm permits and rapid-response teams (Kitat Konenut) neutralized terrorists and saved lives; vehicle thefts fell 20% in 2025.
chapters.arguments_critics: Abandonment of Arab personal safety, record murders, clearance collapse, and political diversion of police resources toward suppressing anti-government demonstrators.

chapters.title: Public Corruption, Good Governance, and Rule of Law
chapters.bottom_line: Administrative norms and the independence of institutional gatekeepers experienced sustained pressure, reflected in Israel's drop to 35th on the global Corruption Perceptions Index and the institutionalization of direct political control over senior civil service appointments.
headlines: Israel dropped to 35th place globally on the 2025 CPI index
Clean governance score declined to 62 out of 100
Search committees eliminated for Civil Service Commissioner selection
chapters.overview: Transparency International's 2025 report downgraded Israel to 35th place globally with a score of 62, warning of democratic erosion and attacks on institutional gatekeepers. Cabinet ministers pursued continuous conflict with the Attorney General, state prosecutors, and ministry legal advisers. The government enacted direct appointment of the Civil Service Commissioner by the Prime Minister without competitive tenders, upheld by an expanded High Court bench in 2026 citing ideological compatibility as a valid metric.
chapters.comparison_prev_gov: The 36th Government respected administrative norms, fortified search committees, and minimized discretionary coalition budgets, raising Israel's CPI score to 64. The 37th Government sought to transform legal advisers into political appointees and bypassed tenders.
chapters.arguments_supporters: Democratic governance demands that elected officials appoint personnel committed to executing their voter mandate, an approach affirmed by the High Court.
chapters.arguments_critics: Dismantling civil service gatekeepers, tender exemptions, and allocating resources along party lines deepens public corruption and undermines institutional trust.

chapters.title: Arab Society and Minorities – Economic and Civic Development
chapters.bottom_line: Civic development programs for Arab society were scaled back, with approximately NIS 2.5 billion cut from Plan 550, while lingering land-use and planning issues in the Druze community remained unresolved.
headlines: Cumulative ~NIS 2.5 billion cut from Five-Year Plan 550 ('Taqaddum')
Hundreds of millions diverted from welfare and education to law enforcement
38% of young Arab men classified as NEET (not in education or work)
chapters.overview: Beyond the violent crime wave, civic and economic relations deteriorated. The NIS 30B five-year plan for Arab development (Resolution 550) was reduced by NIS 2.5B via war budget adjustments. Hundreds of millions earmarked for day-care centers, youth employment, and infrastructure were diverted to the police and Shin Bet. Finance Ministry freezes on municipal balancing grants caused local liquidity crises, while Druze community demands regarding the Kaminitz and Nation-State laws went unanswered.

rows: Proposed fine freezes without law change

chapters.comparison_prev_gov: The 36th Government included the Ra'am party, framed minority development as a vital national economic interest, and initiated Plan 550. The 37th Government adopted an adversarial approach, treating development budgets as political concessions and freezing funds.
chapters.arguments_supporters: Unsupervised cash transfers to Arab municipalities were captured by organized crime cartels winning public tenders; shifting resources to security restores essential order.
chapters.arguments_critics: Freezing civic, educational, and welfare budgets generates an economic vacuum that pushes youth into crime syndicates, representing ideological collective punishment.

chapters.title: Status of Women, Gender Equality, and Personal Safety
chapters.bottom_line: Female representation in executive roles and the civil service declined, marked by an absence from the inner War Cabinet, adjustments to protective electronic monitoring legislation, and an elevated number of domestic violence homicides.
headlines: Female ministers dropped from 9 in the previous government to 5 (~16%)
Female ministry director-generals plummeted from 9 to just 2
Zero female ministers in the inner War Cabinet
chapters.overview: The 37th Government launched with only 5 women among 30+ ministers, while Haredi coalition partners completely excluded women from party lists. Ministry director-generals fell to a single woman initially, rising to two. Throughout the war, the inner War Cabinet was exclusively male. Domestic femicides exceeded 30 victims in 2024 (over 20 in Arab society). The coalition diluted the electronic monitoring bill for domestic abusers with strict evidentiary prerequisites, contrasting with the combat performance of female IDF troops that forced expanded frontline roles.
chapters.comparison_prev_gov: The 36th Government achieved record representation (9 ministers, 9 DGs, first female Attorney General) and pursued the Istanbul Convention. The 37th Government dismantled the Authority for the Advancement of the Status of Women into a political body and excluded women from wartime councils.
chapters.arguments_supporters: Appointments should be based on merit and ideological alignment rather than gender quotas; electronic monitoring modifications prevented potential false complaints during divorce disputes.
chapters.arguments_critics: Excluding women from wartime strategy compromised decision-making and neglected female victims of sexual violence; diluting protection laws endangered battered women.

chapters.title: Foreign Relations, Diplomatic Standing, and Legal Arena
chapters.bottom_line: Israel maintained crucial defense and operational intelligence cooperation with the United States, but experienced significant strain in its broader diplomatic and international legal standing, highlighted by ICC arrest warrants and selective European arms embargoes.
headlines: ICC arrest warrants issued against Israel's Prime Minister and former Defense Minister
ICJ genocide proceedings and selective European arms embargoes
Unprecedented US operational airlift and CENTCOM intercept coalition
chapters.overview: In November 2024, the International Criminal Court (ICC) issued arrest warrants for Prime Minister Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Gallant over the Gaza war. Concurrently, South Africa brought genocide allegations before the International Court of Justice (ICJ). Spain, Ireland, and Norway unilaterally recognized a Palestinian state, and several European allies imposed selective arms restrictions. Conversely, US defense assistance was historic, featuring an arms airlift and CENTCOM regional interception coordination.

rows: Close working ties; public disputes avoided
Persistent friction, shipment pauses, alongside historic aid
Preserved amidst war; Saudi normalization paused
ICC arrest warrants (Netanyahu & Gallant); ICJ litigation
Selective arms embargoes, unilateral Palestinian recognition

chapters.comparison_prev_gov: The 36th Government restored relations with US Democrats and European partners, deepening regional integration through the Negev Forum. The 37th Government experienced constant friction, rhetoric from far-right ministers, and an erosion of international legitimacy.
chapters.arguments_supporters: The administration demonstrated steadfast resolve against intense international pressure to surrender; the US defense pact and Abraham Accords remained intact.
chapters.arguments_critics: Severe diplomatic failure: the lack of a post-war plan and irresponsible rhetoric squandered normalization with Saudi Arabia, brought international arrest warrants, and caused partial European arms embargoes.

chapters.title: Education System, PISA Scores, and Teacher Shortages
chapters.bottom_line: The education system saw a sharp drop in international PISA scores, alongside teacher shortages and infrastructure gaps, while funding to Haredi schools was expanded without core-curriculum requirements and AI program implementation remained uneven.
headlines: PISA 2025 crash: 38-point drop in reading (2nd sharpest globally)
46% of 15-year-olds struggle below baseline mathematics proficiency
NIS 3.5B added to Haredi school networks while non-compliance fines dropped 45%
chapters.overview: The OECD PISA 2025 scores plunged to historic lows for Israeli 15-year-olds: reading fell 38 points to 436, math dropped 25 points to 433 (30 points below the OECD average), and science fell 23 points to 442. Low achievers surged to 46% in math. The system suffered chronic shortages, with 26% of STEM/English teachers lacking certification. Remote learning during the war revealed 27% of schools lacked adequate digital devices. Meanwhile, the cabinet allocated NIS 3.5B to Haredi schools while halving fines for omitting core subjects.
chapters.comparison_prev_gov: The 36th Government raised teacher starting salaries to NIS 9,000 and created a conditional funding framework with Belz Hasidism requiring core curriculum studies. The 37th Government repealed the conditionality, disbursing funds without academic supervision.
chapters.arguments_supporters: PISA scores reflect war disruption, displacement, and closed schools; the ministry launched a pioneering national AI education plan and fixed wage disparities for religious educators.
chapters.arguments_critics: Evacuated border schools were excluded from the PISA sample; pouring billions into private networks lacking core math and science threatens the future of Israel's tech economy.

chapters.title: Healthcare System, Medical Attrition, and Mental Health
chapters.bottom_line: Physical trauma care operated with high dedication during emergency operations, but the mental health sector experienced unprecedented strain, alongside an acceleration in the departure of experienced medical professionals abroad.
headlines: 1,369 physicians left Israel between 2023 and 2025 (+94% surge)
Net loss of 328 doctors in 2024 alone (2.5x historical baselines)
34% of the population reported symptoms of PTSD (national trauma crisis)
chapters.overview: The war was officially designated a national mental health emergency, with 34% reporting moderate-to-severe PTSD symptoms and over 25,000 recognized as direct psychiatric casualties of hostilities. Concurrently, Tel Aviv University research documented 1,369 doctor departures over three years (+94%). In 2024, Israel lost a net 328 physicians, with 23% being senior department heads and surgeons aged 45+. A public sector psychologist wage deal was signed in 2025 to curb outpatient wait times.
chapters.comparison_prev_gov: The 36th Government focused on pandemic recovery, intern shift reductions, and clinical staffing positions. The 37th Government handled mass casualties with clinical proficiency, but struggled to resolve mental health strain and doctor brain drain.
chapters.arguments_supporters: Hospitals provided world-class mass-casualty surgical trauma care during wartime; mental health budgets were expanded and a major wage agreement for public psychologists was enacted in 2025.
chapters.arguments_critics: Mental health clinics experienced multi-month waitlists; institutional polarization drove an unprecedented medical brain drain that threatens future public hospital capacity.

chapters.title: Welfare, Poverty Rates, and Housing Market
chapters.bottom_line: Social welfare transfers prevented an increase in official poverty rates during the war, but living costs continued to rise, and residential real estate prices resumed an upward trajectory due to construction labor shortages.
headlines: ~900,000 children living below the poverty line (28.0%)
Home prices surged 7.3%–7.7% in 2024 following a slight 2023 dip
Severe shortage of tens of thousands of construction workers
chapters.overview: National individual poverty held flat at 20.7%–20.8%, but Israel retained the second-highest child poverty rate in the OECD (28%). Without welfare transfers, family poverty would reach 34.2%. In real estate, after prices jumped 14.7% in 2022 and contracted 0.7% in 2023 due to rate hikes, home prices rebounded by 7.7% in 2024. The rebound occurred despite high interest rates, driven by construction labor shortages after barring Palestinian workers, lengthening build times.
chapters.comparison_prev_gov: The 36th Government managed sharp housing demand through 'Target Price' lottery subsidies and purchase tax adjustments. The 37th Government failed to resolve post-October 7 labor shortages, constricting housing supply and driving prices up.
chapters.arguments_supporters: Emergency grants and National Insurance safety nets averted acute destitution; poverty rates among Haredi and Arab households even recorded slight declines.
chapters.arguments_critics: Nominal poverty stability ignores real purchasing power erosion; failure to import replacement foreign construction workers pushed home prices up over 7% in 2024.

chapters.title: Social Cohesion, Societal Rifts, and Public Trust
chapters.bottom_line: Measures of social cohesion fell, with trust in the Knesset and government dropping below 20%, while disagreements over the judicial overhaul, conscription, and hostage negotiations added to domestic political divisions.
headlines: Public trust in government collapsed to record lows of 18%–23%
Trust in the Knesset stands at just 15%–18%
Over 80% of citizens report high social and political tension
chapters.overview: Measures of social cohesion and institutional trust reached historical lows. Polarization over the 2023 judicial overhaul led to mass street protests and reserve duty boycott debates. While October 7 sparked initial volunteer unity, rifts widened as the war lengthened over hostage-release strategy, Haredi draft exemptions, and political attacks on the military and judiciary.
chapters.comparison_prev_gov: The 36th Government utilized a broad parity coalition model to calm internal political tensions. The 37th Government governed as an ideological right-wing bloc, pursuing unilateral judicial restructuring that triggered massive domestic backlash.
chapters.arguments_supporters: Polarization was driven by political opposition figures and media reluctant to accept the 2022 election outcome; reserve duty refusal threats in 2023 damaged national deterrence.
chapters.arguments_critics: The administration broke the national social contract through a divisive judicial overhaul, attacked gatekeepers, and prioritized coalition survival over hostage rescue.

chapters.title: Demographics, Migration Trends, and Brain Drain
chapters.bottom_line: Israel experienced a period of elevated net negative migration under the 37th Government, marked by departures of educated, working-age citizens alongside a decline in returning residents and new immigrant arrivals.
headlines: Over 82,700 Israelis emigrated annually in both 2023 and 2024 (2x historical avg)
Net negative migration balance of -58,900 citizens in 2024
52% of 2024 emigrants were native-born Israelis (Sabras)
chapters.overview: Emigration rose from an average of ~40,500/year to over 82,700 annually in 2023 and 2024, driving the net negative balance to -58,900 in 2024. Over 80% of departing citizens were under 40, and PhD holders emigrated at 4.6 times their population proportion. Emigration among tech and healthcare professionals surged, while returning residents fell by 53% and Aliyah dropped from 74,000 in 2022 to 31,100 in 2024.
chapters.comparison_prev_gov: In 2022, a major Aliyah wave from Ukraine and Russia offset emigration. Under the 37th Government, immigration fell by 58% while departures reached historic peaks among established professionals.
chapters.arguments_supporters: Emigration figures include non-integrated arrivals who relocated after receiving passports; departures are natural during war, and rising global antisemitism will spur future Aliyah.
chapters.arguments_critics: Most departures are native-born professionals, engineers, and doctors whose confidence in the economic and social contract was damaged by government policy.

chapters.title: Civil Service, Governance, and National Infrastructure
chapters.bottom_line: The government advanced its approach to ministerial discretion and executive appointments (with legal validation from the High Court), while facing delays on major transit projects in the Tel Aviv metropolitan area and unresolved disputes regarding military conscription legislation.
headlines: High Court approved direct appointment of Civil Service Commissioner without tenders
Multi-year delays to the NIS 150B Tel Aviv Metro subway project
Congestion pricing suspended at Tel Aviv entrances
chapters.overview: The cabinet expanded ministerial authority, eliminating competitive search panels for the Civil Service Commissioner, an action upheld by the High Court in 2026. In transportation, Minister Miri Regev shifted priorities away from the Tel Aviv Metro and congestion pricing toward peripheral highways and rail links. In defense law, failure to pass conscription legislation led to unanimous High Court rulings freezing yeshiva subsidies without enlistment.
chapters.comparison_prev_gov: The 36th Government relied on professional ministry civil servants and advanced metropolitan infrastructure. The 37th Government favored political governance, redirecting resources to peripheral and coalition interests.
chapters.arguments_supporters: Elected ministers bear public accountability and should appoint ideological leaders; investment in peripheral transport rectifies historic under-investment.
chapters.arguments_critics: Politicization damages civil service merit, while delaying the Metro threatens urban traffic gridlock and tens of billions in lost economic output.
